title: Medicine and fasting
hookLine: doctors and scholars on fasting with illness

cards: A clinic waiting room, a few weeks before Ramadan. A woman with diabetes holds a question she's carried all year: can I fast this time? Her doctor has an answer about blood sugar.
Her imam has an answer about the law. What she wants is the two of them in the same room. And the Qur'an had already made space for her, in the very passage that commands the fast.

teach.h: THE EXCEPTION IS IN THE VERSE.
teach.b: The verse that sets the fast carries its own exception. In Surah al-Baqarah, Pickthall's translation reads: "(for) him who is sick among you, or on a journey, (the same) number of other days."
So the person who is ill and doesn't fast isn't breaking the rule. They're following it, and the days can be made up later.
The same verse speaks of a ransom, feeding a person in need, which scholars apply to someone who can't make the days up at all, like a person with a lasting illness.
The next verse gives the reason plainly: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." The hadith add a second thread.

teach.h: YOUR BODY HAS A RIGHT OVER YOU.
teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, hears of a companion who fasts every day and prays all night, and tells him to ease off, because, in paraphrase, your body has a right over you.
And in Sunan Abu Dawud he tells people to seek treatment, since Allah has not made a disease without making a remedy for it. Put those side by side: health is a trust.
The body isn't simply yours to spend down; it's held on someone's behalf. So the question in the clinic isn't how tough are you. It's what will this do to you.

teach.h: A DOCTOR AND A SCHOLAR, TOGETHER.
teach.b: Some scholars hold that the advice of a trustworthy doctor can settle it. They differ in the gray cases: how sick is sick enough, and whether an inhaler or an injection breaks the fast.
That's why the doctor and the imam keep meeting.

how: Muslims who are ill or traveling may leave the Ramadan fast and make up the days later; someone who cannot make them up may feed a person in need instead, and some consult both a doctor and a scholar before the month begins.

o: a rule that sick Muslims still fast, but take medicine at night
the fast's own exception for the sick, and the call to seek a cure
a diet of fasting used in place of a doctor's treatment

games.q: fasting and the body — tap the pairs.
p: the same number of other days

s: a Muslim who is sick and doesn't fast in Ramadan is breaking the rule
the verse that commands the fast says the sick and the traveler fast the same number of other days.
in a hadith in al-Bukhari, the Prophet tells a companion to ease off his fasting
he tells him, in paraphrase, that his body has a right over him.
scholars agree on every medical question about fasting
the gray cases, like inhalers and injections, are where they differ.

games.q: you've been fasting every day and praying all night, and the Prophet hears about it. what does he tell you?
o: keep going: the more, the better.
ease off: your body has a right over you.
games.why: he tells the companion to fast some days and not others, and to sleep as well as pray, because his body has a right over him.

practice: Move your attention slowly up from your feet, noticing where you're tired, sore or tight, without fixing anything yet.
Then ask one honest question: what have I been putting off, a checkup, a prescription, sleep, water, a talk with a doctor?
If you pray, hold your body in mind as something entrusted to you; if you don't, simply hold the one thing you named.

wordCard.voice: Medicine and fasting. The fast of Ramadan carries its own exception for the sick, and the hadith tell people to seek a cure. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the fasting, the word the Qur'an uses when it prescribes the fast (2:183).

carryVoice: Your line: health is a trust. Your body has a right over you, too. Until tomorrow.
